content: Breast self-examination is considered by many women to be an important aspect of their personal healthcare routine. Performing regular self-exams allows women to become familiar with the normal texture and feel of their breast tissue. This familiarity can help them identify any unusual lumps or changes that may warrant further discussion with their healthcare provider. However, there is no universal agreement among medical experts regarding the recommendation of breast self-examinations. The role of these exams in detecting breast cancer or improving survival rates remains uncertain. It is advisable to consult with your healthcare provider to determine whether breast self-examinations are appropriate for you. If you choose to perform breast self-examinations, it is recommended to do so approximately 3 to 5 days after the start of your menstrual period, as this is when the breasts are less tender or lumpy. For women who have gone through menopause, it is best to perform the exam on the same day each month for consistency. To begin, lie down on your back. Place your right hand behind your head. Using the middle fingers of your left hand, gently but firmly press down in small circular motions to examine the entire right breast. Next, while sitting or standing, examine your armpit area, as breast tissue extends into this region. Gently squeeze the nipple to check for any discharge. Repeat the same process on the left breast. To ensure thoroughness, use a systematic pattern, such as circular, wedge-shaped, or vertical strip patterns, to cover all breast tissue. It is important to note that most women have some natural lumps in their breasts. The goal of the self-exam is not to determine what every lump or abnormality is but to identify any new or unusual changes. If you notice anything different, consult your healthcare provider for further evaluation. Some women find it easier to perform the exam in the shower when the skin is soft and wet. However, lying down is generally more effective for examining all areas of the breast tissue. After completing the physical examination, stand in front of a mirror with your arms at your sides. Observe your breasts directly and in the mirror for any changes in skin texture, such as dimpling, puckering, indentations, or skin that resembles the texture of an orange peel. Also, look for changes in shape, contour, or the appearance of the nipple, such as inversion. Repeat this visual inspection with your arms raised above your head. If you notice any changes, report them to your healthcare provider immediately.
